scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9058: I'm on PC0 (20.1.1.x) and I can no longer get through
to PC12 (120.1.1.x) on the far side of the network -- it times out every
single time. This used to work, so something has broken on your side. I have
heard our two sides run on "different routing"; I won't pretend to know what
that means, but whatever connects the two sides is yours to run and it is
clearly not doing its job. Take a look and fix it today, please.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The OSPF core is converged, R11 redistributes
  between OSPF and EIGRP, and PC0 (20.1.1.x) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.x) with 0% loss
  in both directions. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a redistribution / interior-link fault that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC0 cannot reach PC12
across the OSPF/EIGRP core -- is NOT reproducible: the OSPF backbone is converged,
R11 redistributes OSPF<->EIGRP (so the 120.x/EIGRP prefixes appear in the OSPF
RIB and vice versa), and PC0 reaches PC12 (120.1.1.x) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: cross-core reachability is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC0->PC12
path, finds it working, optionally confirms R11's redistribution and the EIGRP
neighbors are up, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a broken
redistribution or a down interior link to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The Kath5 network connecting PC0 (20.1.1.x, in the OSPF domain) to PC12 (120.1.1.x, in the EIGRP domain) is fully operational. The "two sides with different routing" the user described is a deliberate OSPF/EIGRP dual-protocol design: the left side of the network (r1 through r9, r10) runs OSPF, the right side (r12, r13) runs EIGRP AS 100, and r11 is the redistribution boundary router that stitches them together.

r11 is correctly configured as both an OSPF area-3 router (peering with r1 on segment B, 111.0.0.0/8) and an EIGRP AS-100 router (peering with r12 on segment EE and r13 on segment FF). It redistributes EIGRP routes into OSPF (`redistribute eigrp`), which causes r12's 120.0.0.0/8 prefix to appear as a Type-5 AS-external LSA in the OSPF domain. That LSA was confirmed present in r1's LSDB (advertising router 112.1.1.1, metric 20, age ~408 s), and r1 installs the corresponding route in its RIB. For the return direction, r12 carries a kernel default route pointing to r11 (112.1.1.1), so all non-EIGRP destinations are forwarded to r11, which holds an OSPF route to 20.0.0.0/8 via r1.

Direct verification: bidirectional pings between PC0 and PC12 show 0% packet loss; traceroute confirms a clean 3-hop path (r1 → r11 → r12); the r1–r11 OSPF adjacency has been Full for nearly 10 minutes; r11's IP forwarding is enabled and iptables has no rules. No misconfiguration, missing route, ACL, or interface fault was found anywhere in the network. The user's report of connectivity loss is not substantiated by any evidence in the live lab — the network was and is healthy.
